stem: A network team needs per-command authorization for administrators on routers, with full encryption of the management traffic and detailed accounting. Which AAA protocol is BEST?

options.rationale: TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization, and accounting (enabling per-command control), encrypts the entire payload, and is designed for granular device administration.
RADIUS combines authN/authZ and encrypts only the password, making granular per-command control and full encryption weaker than TACACS+.
WEP is a broken wireless encryption standard, not an AAA protocol.
FTP is a file-transfer protocol, unrelated to AAA.

stem: Which statement about classic RADIUS is MOST accurate?

options.text: It uses UDP and encrypts only the password in the access-request
options.rationale: Classic RADIUS runs over UDP and encrypts only the user password, leaving other attributes in the clear.

options.text: It uses TCP and encrypts the entire payload
options.rationale: That describes TACACS+, not RADIUS.

options.text: It is a wireless encryption cipher
options.rationale: RADIUS is an AAA protocol, not a cipher.

options.text: It provides no authentication at all
options.rationale: RADIUS is fundamentally an authentication (and authorization/accounting) protocol.

stem: A company deploys 802.1X so each user authenticates before getting network access. Which back-end AAA protocol is MOST commonly used to support this?

options.rationale: 802.1X typically uses RADIUS as the back-end AAA server to authenticate users/devices onto the network.
SMTP is an email protocol, not an AAA back end.
HTTP is a web protocol, not an 802.1X AAA back end.
Telnet is an insecure remote-terminal protocol, not an AAA service.

stem: Which capability MOST distinguishes TACACS+ from RADIUS?

options.text: TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization, and accounting into independent functions
options.rationale: TACACS+ decouples AAA functions (allowing, e.g., separate per-command authorization), whereas RADIUS combines authentication and authorization.
TACACS+ absolutely authenticates users; it also separates authZ and accounting.
TACACS+ uses TCP, not UDP; RADIUS uses UDP.
TACACS+ encrypts the entire payload, more than RADIUS does.

stem: In the context of RADIUS and TACACS+, 'AAA' stands for which of the following?

options.rationale: AAA denotes Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting — the core services these protocols provide.
This is not the standard AAA expansion.
These are unrelated security functions, not the AAA acronym.
This is not what AAA stands for in this context.

stem: Managing separate local admin accounts on hundreds of network devices is error-prone and inconsistent. What is the BEST improvement?

options.text: Centralize authentication using an AAA server (e.g., TACACS+/RADIUS) so credentials and policy are managed in one place
options.rationale: Centralized AAA replaces per-device local accounts with consistent, centrally managed authentication, authorization, and accounting.

options.text: Configure a different password scheme on each device manually
options.rationale: Per-device manual management is exactly the inconsistent, error-prone situation to fix.

options.text: Remove all authentication from the devices
options.rationale: Removing authentication is a severe security failure.

options.text: Use the same shared password everywhere with no server
options.rationale: A universal shared password destroys accountability and is easily leaked.

stem: Which protocol is MOST accurately described as a modern successor to RADIUS with enhanced capabilities?

options.rationale: Diameter was designed as an evolution of RADIUS, offering improved reliability and features.
Telnet is an insecure terminal protocol, not a RADIUS successor.
WEP is a broken wireless standard, unrelated to AAA succession.
SFTP is a secure file-transfer protocol, not an AAA protocol.

stem: Why is hardening and protecting the central AAA server MOST critical?

options.text: Its compromise could grant an attacker control over authentication/authorization for many systems
options.rationale: A central AAA server is a high-value target; compromising it can undermine access control across everything that relies on it.

options.text: Because it stores the office thermostat settings
options.rationale: AAA servers manage authentication, not building climate.
Badge printing is unrelated to the AAA server's function.

options.text: Because it hosts the company website
options.rationale: An AAA server's criticality is its control over access, not web hosting.

stem: An authentication system needs a central store to look up user accounts and attributes. Which technology MOST commonly serves this role?

options.text: A directory service such as LDAP / Active Directory
options.rationale: Directory services (LDAP/AD) are the standard central identity store queried by authentication systems.
An emailed spreadsheet is not a scalable, secure directory store.
A print queue does not store identities.
DNS resolves names; it is not an identity/attribute store for authentication.

stem: To control and audit the use of shared administrative credentials, which solution is BEST?

options.text: A Privileged Access Management (PAM) system that vaults credentials and records sessions
options.rationale: PAM brokers and vaults privileged credentials, enforces check-out, and records sessions, providing control and accountability over admin access.

options.text: Writing the admin password on a whiteboard
options.rationale: Exposing credentials on a whiteboard is grossly insecure.

options.text: Emailing the admin password to the whole team
options.rationale: Broadly sharing credentials destroys accountability and control.
Disabling logging removes the accountability PAM is meant to provide.

stem: Which pairing of transport protocols is MOST correct for these AAA protocols?

options.text: RADIUS uses UDP; TACACS+ uses TCP
options.rationale: RADIUS runs over UDP while TACACS+ runs over TCP — a standard exam distinction.

options.text: RADIUS uses TCP; TACACS+ uses UDP
options.rationale: This reverses reality; RADIUS is UDP and TACACS+ is TCP.
Neither uses ICMP for AAA transport.

options.text: Both are transport-agnostic and use no protocol
options.rationale: Both use specific transports (UDP and TCP respectively).

stem: A security requirement mandates that AAA management traffic be fully encrypted, not just the password. Which protocol MOST directly meets this?

options.rationale: TACACS+ encrypts the entire payload, satisfying full-encryption requirements, unlike RADIUS which encrypts only the password.
Classic RADIUS encrypts only the password, leaving other attributes exposed.
Telnet is cleartext and not an AAA protocol.
HTTP is unencrypted and not an AAA protocol.

stem: A switch authenticates to a RADIUS server using a shared secret. What is the BEST practice for that secret?

options.text: Use a strong, unique shared secret and protect it, rotating it periodically
options.rationale: Strong, unique, protected, and rotated shared secrets secure the client-server AAA channel against compromise.

options.text: Use 'secret' as the shared secret everywhere
options.rationale: A weak, reused secret is trivially guessed and compromises all devices using it.
Publishing the secret defeats its purpose.

options.text: Never set a shared secret at all
options.rationale: Omitting the shared secret leaves the AAA channel unauthenticated/unprotected.

stem: A colleague suggests using RADIUS to provide web single sign-on across external SaaS applications. Which correction is MOST accurate?

options.text: RADIUS is a network-access AAA protocol; web SSO/federation across SaaS uses SAML or OIDC
options.rationale: RADIUS handles network-access AAA (e.g., 802.1X/VPN), whereas cross-application web SSO/federation is done with SAML or OIDC.

options.text: RADIUS is the standard for SaaS web federation
options.rationale: SaaS web federation uses SAML/OIDC, not RADIUS.
They serve different purposes: AAA network access vs. web federation.

options.text: Web SSO cannot be done with any protocol
options.rationale: Web SSO is readily achieved with SAML/OIDC.

stem: TACACS+ is most closely associated with which origin?

options.rationale: TACACS+ is a Cisco protocol commonly used for device administration AAA.

options.text: A wireless encryption standard from IEEE
options.rationale: TACACS+ is an AAA protocol, not a wireless encryption standard.
TACACS+ is unrelated to email transport.
TACACS+ is not a certificate format.

stem: The 'accounting' function in AAA MOST directly supports which security goal?

options.text: Accountability — recording what authenticated users did for auditing
options.rationale: AAA accounting logs user activity/sessions, supporting accountability and audit trails.
Accounting logs actions; it does not encrypt stored data.
Accounting is a logging function, not physical security.
Accounting has no effect on bandwidth.

stem: A limitation cited for classic RADIUS in granular device administration is MOST accurately which of the following?

options.text: It combines authentication and authorization, making fine-grained per-command control harder
options.rationale: Because RADIUS couples authN and authZ, it is less suited to the per-command authorization granularity that TACACS+'s separation enables.
RADIUS authenticates users; the limitation is coupling of authN/authZ, not inability to authenticate.
RADIUS actually encrypts less (only the password), not too much.
RADIUS uses UDP, not TCP.

stem: If the single AAA server fails, no one can authenticate to network devices. What is the BEST design improvement?

options.text: Deploy redundant AAA servers so authentication continues if one fails
options.rationale: Redundant/highly available AAA servers remove the single point of failure so authentication remains available during an outage.

options.text: Remove authentication so failures never block access
options.rationale: Removing authentication eliminates access control entirely — an unacceptable trade.

options.text: Use one server with no backup to keep it simple
options.rationale: A single server is exactly the single point of failure described.
Shutting down the network is not a viable availability solution.

stem: For authenticating remote VPN users against a central identity store across mixed-vendor equipment, which AAA protocol is BEST suited?

options.text: RADIUS, which is widely supported across vendors for network-access AAA
options.rationale: RADIUS's broad cross-vendor support makes it well suited to VPN/network-access authentication in mixed environments.

options.text: A Cisco-only protocol that other vendors cannot use
options.rationale: A single-vendor protocol is a poor fit for mixed-vendor equipment; RADIUS's interoperability is the advantage.
Telnet is not an AAA protocol.
SMTP is an email protocol, not an AAA service.

stem: Which factor is LEAST relevant when implementing a centralized authentication system?

options.text: The wall color of the server room
options.rationale: Server-room wall color has no bearing on the authentication system's implementation or security, making it least relevant.

options.text: Protecting the AAA server and its shared secrets
options.rationale: Securing the AAA server and secrets is critical to the implementation.

options.text: Choosing RADIUS vs TACACS+ based on requirements
options.rationale: Selecting the right protocol for the use case is a key implementation decision.
Redundancy is important to avoid a single point of authentication failure.
